raw_evidence.label: What the L2M Report is
raw_evidence.content: The NBA Last Two Minute Report (L2M) is a public, play-by-play audit document that grades every referee decision in the last two minutes of close games. Originally triggered only in games within three points at the two-minute mark, the scope later expanded. Each play is categorized as CC (Correct Call), CNC (Correct Non-Call), IC (Incorrect Call), or INC (Incorrect Non-Call). The league posts these PDFs the next day on official.nba.com with the referees' names attached — making it one of the most transparent real-time officiating audits in any major pro league.

raw_evidence.label: Origin — March 2015, after the Donaghy scandal
raw_evidence.content: The NBA began issuing L2M Reports on March 1, 2015. The program was born out of a transparency push by new commissioner Adam Silver, arriving nearly eight years after the 2007 Tim Donaghy betting scandal in which a sitting NBA referee pleaded guilty to betting on games he officiated and was sentenced to 15 months in federal prison. Sports betting was also on the cusp of becoming legal in the United States — PASPA would be struck down in 2018 — and the league publicly needed to show it took officiating integrity seriously. The L2M was positioned as a credibility instrument, not an internal training tool.

raw_evidence.label: Overall CC / CNC / IC / INC split
raw_evidence.content: Of 25,057 NBA-reviewed late-game decisions from March 2015 through June 2018, the league classified 29.58% as Correct Calls (CC, 7,412 plays), 61.65% as Correct Non-Calls (CNC, 15,448 plays), 0.96% as Incorrect Calls (IC, 240 plays), and 7.81% as Incorrect Non-Calls (INC, 1,957 plays). Overall correctness is 91.23%. Missed whistles (INC) outnumber wrongful whistles (IC) by 8.2 to 1 — the league's late-game errors are overwhelmingly errors of omission.

raw_evidence.label: Overall CC / CNC / IC / INC split
raw_evidence.content: Of 25,057 NBA-reviewed late-game decisions from March 2015 through June 2018, the league classified 29.58% as Correct Calls (CC, 7,412 plays), 61.65% as Correct Non-Calls (CNC, 15,448 plays), 0.96% as Incorrect Calls (IC, 240 plays), and 7.81% as Incorrect Non-Calls (INC, 1,957 plays). Overall correctness is 91.23%. Missed whistles (INC) outnumber wrongful whistles (IC) by 8.2 to 1 — the league's late-game errors are overwhelmingly errors of omission.

print("=== ana_01 ===")
vc = df['review_decision'].value_counts()
total = vc.sum()
for k in ['CC', 'CNC', 'IC', 'INC']:
    print(f"{k}: {vc[k]} ({vc[k]/total*100:.2f}%)")
correct = vc['CC'] + vc['CNC']
incorrect = vc['IC'] + vc['INC']
print(f"\nTOTAL correct (CC+CNC): {correct} ({correct/total*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"TOTAL incorrect (IC+INC): {incorrect} ({incorrect/total*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"\n-- breakdown of incorrect --")
print(f"IC (wrong whistles): {vc['IC']} ({vc['IC']/incorrect*100:.1f}% of all errors)")
print(f"INC (missed whistles): {vc['INC']} ({vc['INC']/incorrect*100:.1f}% of all errors)")
print(f"\nINC/IC ratio: {vc['INC']/vc['IC']:.2f} (missed calls are {vc['INC']/vc['IC']:.1f}x more common than wrong whistles)")
# end ana_01

raw_evidence.label: Error rate by call type
raw_evidence.content: Error rates vary wildly by call type. Defensive 3-second violations are missed 63.6% of the time (140 INC of 220 total), and traveling violations are missed 43.9% of the time (237 INC of 539 total). At the other extreme, shooting fouls and personal fouls — the bread-and-butter calls — are officiated correctly 93-95% of the time. The obscure, process-heavy violations are where the crew gets sloppy; the high-consequence contact calls get attention.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_03 ===")
ct = df.groupby('call_type')['review_decision'].value_counts().unstack(fill_value=0)
for col in ['CC', 'CNC', 'IC', 'INC']:
    if col not in ct.columns:
        ct[col] = 0
ct['total'] = ct[['CC', 'CNC', 'IC', 'INC']].sum(axis=1)
ct['incorrect'] = ct['IC'] + ct['INC']
ct['incorrect_pct'] = ct['incorrect'] / ct['total'] * 100
# Filter to call types with at least 100 decisions for meaningful rates
top = ct[ct['total'] >= 100].sort_values('incorrect_pct', ascending=False)
print("Call types with ≥100 plays, sorted by error %:")
for idx, row in top.iterrows():
    print(f"  {idx:40s} total={int(row['total']):5d}  IC={int(row['IC']):4d}  INC={int(row['INC']):4d}  error_pct={row['incorrect_pct']:.1f}%")
# end ana_03

sentences.summary: det_07: Benchmark: what 'acceptable' officiating looks like. Source: L2M Data Archive (https://atlhawksfanatic.github.io/L2M/) Facts: 1,476 games analyzed; 26,822 total reviewed plays

raw_evidence.label: Benchmark: what 'acceptable' officiating looks like
raw_evidence.content: The NBA itself has said that ~95% of last-two-minute calls are correct — a figure that fans find cold comfort when the 5% decides championships. In the L2M dataset the overall incorrect rate is 8.2% (2,197 incorrect decisions out of 26,822 reviewed plays, across 1,476 games — roughly 1.49 errors per game), which includes both incorrect calls (whistles that shouldn't have blown) and incorrect non-calls (whistles that should have). The NBA has consistently argued the L2M undercounts correctness because every CNC (correct non-call) is only flagged if someone requested review — so the denominator of 'things the refs got right' is larger than it looks. Still: in games where the lead is three points or fewer, an average of 1.49 meaningful mistakes per game is the baseline a reader needs.

raw_evidence.label: Error rate cut in half over four seasons
raw_evidence.content: The league has measurably gotten better. Error rate fell from 13.03% in the partial 2014-15 season to 11.52% in 2015-16, 8.62% in 2016-17, and 6.15% in 2017-18 — less than half the inaugural rate. Errors per game dropped from 1.84 to 1.27 on the same trajectory. Either the league's expansion of reviewed eligibility in 2017-18 is catching easier decisions (diluting the error rate), the crew is actually improving under scrutiny, or both. Absolute IC and INC counts also fell even as total reviewed plays rose from 6,830 to 9,698.

print("=== ana_14 ===")
season_stats = df.groupby('season')['review_decision'].value_counts().unstack(fill_value=0)
for col in ['CC', 'CNC', 'IC', 'INC']:
    if col not in season_stats.columns:
        season_stats[col] = 0
season_stats['total'] = season_stats[['CC', 'CNC', 'IC', 'INC']].sum(axis=1)
season_stats['incorrect'] = season_stats['IC'] + season_stats['INC']
season_stats['incorrect_pct'] = season_stats['incorrect'] / season_stats['total'] * 100
season_stats['games'] = df.groupby('season')['game_id'].nunique()
season_stats['errors_per_game'] = season_stats['incorrect'] / season_stats['games']
season_stats = season_stats.sort_index()
print(f"{'season':10s} {'games':>6s} {'plays':>6s} {'CC':>5s} {'CNC':>6s} {'IC':>4s} {'INC':>5s} {'err%':>6s} {'err/g':>7s}")
for s, row in season_stats.iterrows():

# end ana_14

raw_evidence.label: Scott Foster — 'The Extender', 'Agent 48'
raw_evidence.content: Referee Scott Foster has become the lightning rod of L2M-era officiating criticism. In anonymous player surveys by the Los Angeles Times (2016) and The Athletic (2023, n=108), Foster was voted the worst referee in the league. Nicknamed 'Agent 48' and 'the Extender' because trailing teams in playoff series have an unusually high win rate when he officiates. He received 134 phone calls from disgraced referee Tim Donaghy during Donaghy's betting period — though a 2008 federal investigation cleared him of wrongdoing. Chris Paul has an openly personal feud with Foster dating to 2018: 'It's personal. The league knows, everybody knows, there's been a meeting.' Foster is the perfect test case for the L2M data — either the numbers will damn him or exonerate him.

raw_evidence.content: Referee Scott Foster has become the lightning rod of L2M-era officiating criticism. In anonymous player surveys by the Los Angeles Times (2016) and The Athletic (2023, n=108), Foster was voted the worst referee in the league. Nicknamed 'Agent 48' and 'the Extender' because trailing teams in playoff series have an unusually high win rate when he officiates. He received 134 phone calls from disgraced referee Tim Donaghy during Donaghy's betting period — though a 2008 federal investigation cleared him of wrongdoing. Chris Paul has an openly personal feud with Foster dating to 2018: 'It's personal. The league knows, everybody knows, there's been a meeting.' Foster is the perfect test case for the L2M data — either the numbers will damn him or exonerate him.

raw_evidence.label: Scott Foster — 'The Extender', 'Agent 48'
raw_evidence.content: Referee Scott Foster has become the lightning rod of L2M-era officiating criticism. In anonymous player surveys by the Los Angeles Times (2016) and The Athletic (2023, n=108), Foster was voted the worst referee in the league. Nicknamed 'Agent 48' and 'the Extender' because trailing teams in playoff series have an unusually high win rate when he officiates. He received 134 phone calls from disgraced referee Tim Donaghy during Donaghy's betting period — though a 2008 federal investigation cleared him of wrongdoing. Chris Paul has an openly personal feud with Foster dating to 2018: 'It's personal. The league knows, everybody knows, there's been a meeting.' Foster is the perfect test case for the L2M data — either the numbers will damn him or exonerate him.

raw_evidence.label: Most-worked referees and their error rates
raw_evidence.content: Scott Foster — the referee voted worst in the league by anonymous player surveys — leads all officials with 94 L2M-reviewed games and 1,599 plays judged. His error rate of 9.82% is noticeably above the league median of 8.83% for refs with 40+ games. Among the top 15 most-worked refs, Tom Washington (10.36%), Leroy Richardson (10.18%), and Josh Tiven (10.28%) have higher error rates than Foster; Bill Kennedy (6.85%) and Tony Brothers (8.30%) have notably lower rates. The spread among the league's most-used referees is narrow but real.
raw_evidence.code:
# Games per ref (unique game-ref combos)
games_per_ref = ref_long.groupby('ref')['game_id'].nunique()
# Error counts per ref (decisions observed as a crew member)
ref_decisions = ref_long.groupby('ref')['review_decision'].value_counts().unstack(fill_value=0)
for col in ['CC', 'CNC', 'IC', 'INC']:
    if col not in ref_decisions.columns:
        ref_decisions[col] = 0
ref_decisions['total_plays'] = ref_decisions[['CC', 'CNC', 'IC', 'INC']].sum(axis=1)
ref_decisions['incorrect'] = ref_decisions['IC'] + ref_decisions['INC']
ref_decisions['incorrect_pct'] = ref_decisions['incorrect'] / ref_decisions['total_plays'] * 100
ref_decisions['games'] = games_per_ref

# Filter to refs who worked ≥ 40 games (meaningful sample)
eligible = ref_decisions[ref_decisions['games'] >= 40].copy()
eligible = eligible.sort_values('games', ascending=False)

print(f"Refs with ≥40 L2M games: {len(eligible)}")
print(f"\n-- Top 15 by games worked --")
print(f"{'ref':25s} {'games':>6s} {'plays':>6s} {'IC':>4s} {'INC':>4s} {'err_pct':>8s}")
for ref, row in eligible.head(15).iterrows():

raw_evidence.label: Home court advantage and referee bias
raw_evidence.content: Multiple independent analyses of the L2M data have found that home teams benefit from referee decisions: more infractions are correctly called on away teams, away teams are the victim of more incorrect calls, and home teams are the beneficiary of more incorrect non-calls. A Harvard Sports Analysis piece and The Pudding's 2017 investigation both found a small but statistically significant home-court bias in late-game calls. A 2023 Nature Scientific Reports paper on implicit referee bias used NBA referees as a testbed and confirmed the pattern. Yet other studies of smaller samples find no significant bias — the truth is closer to 'small, real, uneven.'

raw_evidence.label: Home vs away team error split (no meaningful bias)
raw_evidence.content: Across 2,165 errors where the hurt team is identifiable, the home team was disadvantaged 1,080 times (49.88%) and the away team 1,085 times (50.12%). A five-call difference across the entire four-season dataset. On incorrect calls (wrongful whistles, n=225) there is a faint lean toward hurting the home team (52.89% home vs 47.11% away — 13 extra calls); on incorrect non-calls (missed whistles, n=1,940) away teams are hurt slightly more (50.46% vs 49.54%). Neither lean is statistically meaningful. The folklore that L2M data proves home-court bias is not supported in this time window.
raw_evidence.code:
df['com_is_home'] = df.apply(lambda r: r['committing_team'] == r['home'], axis=1)

# --- ana_08: who gets disadvantaged more — home or away? (by review_decision type) ---
print("=== ana_08 ===")
# For IC (incorrect calls — wrongful whistle), the disadvantaged party is the team unfairly called against
# For INC (incorrect non-calls — missed whistle), the disadvantaged party is the team that deserved a foul called for them
# So in both error types: a "disadvantaged = home" means the home team got hurt by the error

errors = df[df['review_decision'].isin(['IC', 'INC'])].copy()
errors = errors.dropna(subset=['disadvantaged_team'])
errors_home_hurt = (errors['disadvantaged_team'] == errors['home']).sum()
errors_away_hurt = (errors['disadvantaged_team'] == errors['away']).sum()
total_errors = errors_home_hurt + errors_away_hurt
print(f"Total errors with known disadvantaged team: {total_errors}")
print(f"Home team hurt by error:  {errors_home_hurt} ({errors_home_hurt/total_errors*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"Away team hurt by error:  {errors_away_hurt} ({errors_away_hurt/total_errors*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"Delta (away - home): {errors_away_hurt - errors_home_hurt} extra errors hurting away teams")

# Split by error type
for etype in ['IC', 'INC']:
    sub = errors[errors['review_decision'] == etype]
    home_hurt = (sub['disadvantaged_team'] == sub['home']).sum()
    away_hurt = (sub['disadvantaged_team'] == sub['away']).sum()
    tot = home_hurt + away_hurt
    print(f"\n{etype}: total={tot}")
    print(f"  home hurt: {home_hurt} ({home_hurt/tot*100:.2f}%)")
    print(f"  away hurt: {away_hurt} ({away_hurt/tot*100:.2f}%)")
# end ana_08

# --- ana_09: correct calls — no bias expected ---
print("\n=== ana_09 ===")

raw_evidence.label: Home vs away team error split (no meaningful bias)
raw_evidence.content: Across 2,165 errors where the hurt team is identifiable, the home team was disadvantaged 1,080 times (49.88%) and the away team 1,085 times (50.12%). A five-call difference across the entire four-season dataset. On incorrect calls (wrongful whistles, n=225) there is a faint lean toward hurting the home team (52.89% home vs 47.11% away — 13 extra calls); on incorrect non-calls (missed whistles, n=1,940) away teams are hurt slightly more (50.46% vs 49.54%). Neither lean is statistically meaningful. The folklore that L2M data proves home-court bias is not supported in this time window.
raw_evidence.code:
df['com_is_home'] = df.apply(lambda r: r['committing_team'] == r['home'], axis=1)

# --- ana_08: who gets disadvantaged more — home or away? (by review_decision type) ---
print("=== ana_08 ===")
# For IC (incorrect calls — wrongful whistle), the disadvantaged party is the team unfairly called against
# For INC (incorrect non-calls — missed whistle), the disadvantaged party is the team that deserved a foul called for them
# So in both error types: a "disadvantaged = home" means the home team got hurt by the error

errors = df[df['review_decision'].isin(['IC', 'INC'])].copy()
errors = errors.dropna(subset=['disadvantaged_team'])
errors_home_hurt = (errors['disadvantaged_team'] == errors['home']).sum()
errors_away_hurt = (errors['disadvantaged_team'] == errors['away']).sum()
total_errors = errors_home_hurt + errors_away_hurt
print(f"Total errors with known disadvantaged team: {total_errors}")
print(f"Home team hurt by error:  {errors_home_hurt} ({errors_home_hurt/total_errors*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"Away team hurt by error:  {errors_away_hurt} ({errors_away_hurt/total_errors*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"Delta (away - home): {errors_away_hurt - errors_home_hurt} extra errors hurting away teams")

# Split by error type
for etype in ['IC', 'INC']:
    sub = errors[errors['review_decision'] == etype]
    home_hurt = (sub['disadvantaged_team'] == sub['home']).sum()
    away_hurt = (sub['disadvantaged_team'] == sub['away']).sum()
    tot = home_hurt + away_hurt
    print(f"\n{etype}: total={tot}")
    print(f"  home hurt: {home_hurt} ({home_hurt/tot*100:.2f}%)")
    print(f"  away hurt: {away_hurt} ({away_hurt/tot*100:.2f}%)")
# end ana_08

# --- ana_09: correct calls — no bias expected ---
print("\n=== ana_09 ===")

Source: Using Data Science to Investigate NBA Referee Myths - Sports X Analytics (https://medium.com/sports-x-analytics/using-data-science-to-breakdown-the-nba-l2) Facts: LeBron James 2015-2019: 17 more disadvantaged than advantaged calls; James Harden: 708 L2M appearances, 35 advantaged vs 24 disadvantaged (9.7% advantage rate) Source: Do NBA Superstars Really Get All the Calls? - SportsRaid (https://medium.com/sportsraid/do-nba-superstars-really-get-all-the-calls-basketb) Facts: Fan perception of star treatment not consistently supported by L2M data

raw_evidence.label: The superstar call myth
raw_evidence.content: Fan folklore holds that superstars — LeBron, Harden, Curry — get favorable whistles. The L2M data has repeatedly been used to test this. Findings are mixed and counter-intuitive. LeBron James from 2015-2019 actually received 17 more disadvantaged calls than advantaged ones — a net negative. James Harden, in contrast, had the most L2M appearances (708) with 35 advantaged and 24 disadvantaged calls (9.7% advantage rate). The superstar effect is real for some players but inverted for others. The L2M is one of the few datasets where this can actually be tested — most foul-call data doesn't track correctness.

raw_evidence.label: Players most disadvantaged by referee errors
raw_evidence.content: Andrew Wiggins has the most negative net in the league: 22 times disadvantaged by errors, 7 times the beneficiary — a net of -15 calls over his 335 L2M appearances. Damian Lillard (-14), Isaiah Thomas (-13), Kemba Walker (-12), and Gordon Hayward (-11) round out the top five. LeBron James also tilts negative (25 disadvantaged, 20 committing — net -5) across 477 appearances. These are guards and wings — the kind of players whose close-game drives are most likely to draw hard-to-officiate contact. Superstar treatment, if it exists, is not landing here.

raw_evidence.label: The superstar call myth
raw_evidence.content: Fan folklore holds that superstars — LeBron, Harden, Curry — get favorable whistles. The L2M data has repeatedly been used to test this. Findings are mixed and counter-intuitive. LeBron James from 2015-2019 actually received 17 more disadvantaged calls than advantaged ones — a net negative. James Harden, in contrast, had the most L2M appearances (708) with 35 advantaged and 24 disadvantaged calls (9.7% advantage rate). The superstar effect is real for some players but inverted for others. The L2M is one of the few datasets where this can actually be tested — most foul-call data doesn't track correctness.

raw_evidence.label: Benchmark: what 'acceptable' officiating looks like
raw_evidence.content: The NBA itself has said that ~95% of last-two-minute calls are correct — a figure that fans find cold comfort when the 5% decides championships. In the L2M dataset the overall incorrect rate is 8.2% (2,197 incorrect decisions out of 26,822 reviewed plays, across 1,476 games — roughly 1.49 errors per game), which includes both incorrect calls (whistles that shouldn't have blown) and incorrect non-calls (whistles that should have). The NBA has consistently argued the L2M undercounts correctness because every CNC (correct non-call) is only flagged if someone requested review — so the denominator of 'things the refs got right' is larger than it looks. Still: in games where the lead is three points or fewer, an average of 1.49 meaningful mistakes per game is the baseline a reader needs.

raw_evidence.label: Error rate by seconds-left (the buzzer effect reversed)
raw_evidence.content: Intuition says mistakes get worse under pressure as the clock winds down. The data says the opposite: error rate drops to 6.62% in the last 10 seconds (27 IC, 236 INC out of 3,972 decisions), compared with 8-10% everywhere else in the two-minute window. The 40-49 second bucket has the single highest error rate at 10.07%. One plausible reading: referees call fewer speculative whistles — more ball stays inbounds, more timeouts are used, more action is dead — as the buzzer approaches, so the decisions that survive are easier ones.

raw_evidence.label: Benchmark: what 'acceptable' officiating looks like
raw_evidence.content: The NBA itself has said that ~95% of last-two-minute calls are correct — a figure that fans find cold comfort when the 5% decides championships. In the L2M dataset the overall incorrect rate is 8.2% (2,197 incorrect decisions out of 26,822 reviewed plays, across 1,476 games — roughly 1.49 errors per game), which includes both incorrect calls (whistles that shouldn't have blown) and incorrect non-calls (whistles that should have). The NBA has consistently argued the L2M undercounts correctness because every CNC (correct non-call) is only flagged if someone requested review — so the denominator of 'things the refs got right' is larger than it looks. Still: in games where the lead is three points or fewer, an average of 1.49 meaningful mistakes per game is the baseline a reader needs.

raw_evidence.content: The National Basketball Referees Association (NBRA) has publicly asked the league to kill the L2M program.
